````text
# codemap

Ask how your code works and get a map you can point at. Claude explores the repo and drafts the answer as a graph of
areas, steps and labeled arrows. A plain program checks every box and arrow against the real code before you see it.
Then you can take a walkthrough, select any part and ask about it, and fix a missing connection right from the map.

Design: [Codemap v1 Design](https://claude.ai/artifact/55L8tokprGe61qtfpDXJ5h).

## Use it

```
npm i
npm run build                                              # the viewer
npm run codemap -- "What happens when a user signs up?" --repo /path/to/your/repo
```

It prints a link (`http://127.0.0.1:4317/m/<id>?t=<token>`) and opens it. Maps are saved in the target repo under
`.codemap/maps/`; commit them to share. Other commands:

```
npm run codemap -- open --repo <dir>            # maps already made in that repo
npm run codemap -- check <map-id> --repo <dir>  # re-check a saved map against the code (exit 1 if a claim fails)
```

Options: `--port <n>` (default 4317), `--no-open`, `--model <id>` (default `claude-opus-5-5`, or `CODEMAP_MODEL`).

Claude access: an `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, or a logged-in Claude Code (the Agent SDK uses it).

To put `codemap` on your PATH: `npm link -w @codemap/server`.

### From a coding agent

`integrations/skills/codemap/SKILL.md` is a skill in the standard `SKILL.md` format. Copy the `codemap` folder into
`.claude/skills/` (Claude Code), `.agents/skills/` (Codex, Gemini CLI) or `.cursor/skills/` (Cursor). Your agent then
runs codemap when you ask how something works, and hands you the link.

### Try it without a model

```
npm run preview
```

The real server and viewer on a throwaway copy of the care-app fixture, with a scripted stand-in for Claude. Nothing
is sent anywhere. Useful for UI work and demos.

## How it works

1. **Make a map.** A deterministic scan gives Claude a head start (entry points, routes, which requests hit which
   routes, which tables are written). Claude explores with Read/Grep/Glob only and returns the map in a fixed format.
2. **Check every claim.** `check()` re-reads each cited line, verifies calls, requests and imports against code facts,
   and re-runs the search behind every "nothing does X". Claude gets up to two rounds to fix what didn't hold. Anything
   still unconfirmed is shown with a "?", never hidden.
3. **Explore.** The viewer draws areas, steps, labeled arrows and red dashed gaps, with a walkthrough Claude wrote. Select
   anything and ask: answers come at three depths (concept, how it works, code) with their sources. Claude explores
   further when the map isn't enough; what it finds is drawn only if it passes the checker.
4. **Fix from the map.** Ask for a change and Claude proposes a fix, drawn as a green dashed arrow next to the exact diff.
   Nothing changes until you approve. Then codemap writes exactly that change (refusing if the files changed since),
   re-checks the map, and offers Undo.

## Packages

| Package | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `@codemap/facts` | What the code says, read deterministically: imports, symbols, calls, routes, table reads and writes, fetch → route links. TS/JS via oxc, Python and Go via tree-sitter. Carried over from the hackathon harness with its tests. |
| `@codemap/core` | The map format (`parseMap`), the checker (`check`), map edits, and read-only repo access that never reads secrets. |
| `@codemap/server` | The Claude map maker and explainer (Agent SDK, read-only tools, secret guard), fixes, the local HTTP/WebSocket server, and the `codemap` CLI. |
| `@codemap/viewer` | The React Flow + ELK viewer: the map, walkthrough, answers, fixes and the input bar. |

## Development

```
npm test           # every package (no model calls; Claude is scripted in tests)
npm run typecheck
npm run build      # the viewer bundle the server serves
```

`packages/core/test/fixtures/care-app` is the reference app: staff convert a patient, the app announces it, nothing
listens, so the welcome email never goes out. `care-app.map.json` is the map of that question.
````

````text
# codemap

A map you can point at and ask about, for code you didn't write yourself. Read `README.md`, then `HANDOFF.md` (who it's
for, what users asked for, the decisions and why, what's next, gotchas). The design lives in the "Codemap v1 Design"
artifact (link in both).

## Rules

- **The model writes, the code decides.** Nothing reaches the screen without passing `check()` in `@codemap/core`. A
  model never sets a claim's status; the checker computes it from the repo every time.
- **One checker, every call site.** Publishing a map, every answer, reopening a saved map, and after a fix all call the
  same `check()`. Don't fork its logic.
- **"Nothing does X" is a claim too.** Absences carry the search that proves them, and the checker reruns it.
- **The map format is the one-way door.** Change `packages/core/src/format.ts` deliberately, with tests. Everything
  else (generator, viewer, explainer) is replaceable behind it.
- **Read-only unless approved.** Codemap writes to a target repo only under `.codemap/`, and edits product code only
  after the user approves a fix previewed on the map. Claude never edits: it proposes, and `applyFix` writes exactly
  the approved change, refusing if the files changed since. Only one agent edits at a time.
- **All model calls go through one `Agent`** (`packages/server/src/agent.ts`): read-only tools, the secret guard,
  structured output. Tests inject a scripted `Agent`; `npm test` never calls a model.
- **Never read secrets.** `.env*`, keys and similar files are refused by `createRepoReader` and left out of searches.
  Paths in maps must stay inside the repo.
- **No model calls in `@codemap/facts` or the checker.** They must be deterministic and fast.
- **Plain English in anything a person reads.** Jargon belongs in the code tab and in engineering detail.
- TypeScript strict, with `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`. Vitest. Pin dependency versions exactly.
- **Don't guess Agent SDK or Claude Code APIs** (channels, MCP Apps, hooks). Check the docs first.

## Commands

```
npm i
npm test             # every package, no model calls
npm run typecheck
npm run build        # viewer bundle (the server serves packages/viewer/dist)
npm run preview      # whole app with a scripted Claude, on a copy of the care-app fixture
npm run codemap -- "<question>" --repo <dir>   # the real thing (uses Claude)
```

## Context

- Packages: `facts` (deterministic code facts) → `core` (format, checker, map edits, safe repo reads) → `server`
  (maker, explainer, fixes, HTTP/WebSocket server, CLI) → `viewer` (React Flow + ELK). The viewer imports server and
  core types only (`import type`), never their runtime code.
- The agent skill is `integrations/skills/codemap/SKILL.md`.
- `@codemap/facts` was carried over from the hackathon harness (`../Speedhacks-project/packages/core`) with its tests.
  The harness is a separate project; don't import from it or edit it from here.
- Test fixtures: `packages/facts/test/{alias-repo,fixture-py,fixture-go}` and `packages/core/test/fixtures/care-app`
  (planted missing listener). Its `.env` holds a fake key for the secret-refusal tests.
----
# Handoff: where codemap came from, what's decided, what's next

Context for anyone (person or agent) picking codemap up. The code and `README.md` say *what* exists; this says *why*,
what was learned along the way, and what's still open. As of 2026-11-02.

## 1. The problem

When you build mostly by directing AI agents, you lose your model of the system. Fixes become band-aids: each change is
judged locally ("did the error go away?") rather than against how the system is meant to work, and nobody notices the
same spot being patched five times. Call it **comprehension debt**: code that exists but that no person understands.

The founding example is real. On an EHR workflow builder (care journeys, journey templates, automations such as "send
this email after the patient converts"), the concepts kept getting rewired, and the frontend looked finished. It was
impossible to tell how the backend was wired, or whether it was wired at all. *"I just trusted what I saw on the
frontend."*

## 2. Who it's for

- **Main user: semi-technical builders who ship with agents.** They know enough to act on what a map shows ("nothing
  listens for this event" is obviously a bug), but can't hold the whole system in their head. This group is growing
  fastest.
- **Not fully non-technical people.** They want "make it work and don't make me think about the backend", which works
  against the product. They're also mostly inside Lovable, Replit or Bolt, which own the screen.
- **Not senior engineers, mostly.** They already hold the model. The exception is an unfamiliar codebase.
- **Buyer later: teams and eng leads** worried about agent-written code nobody understands.
- **Framing:** it's not "leveling the playing field". It's "stay in control of what your agent builds, and get better
  at it as you go."

## 3. What people said (Oct 2026 interviews)

- **Jay** struggles with UX iteration; that's a different product, so leave it out. Separately, he worries whether V1 will
  hold up for V2 and V3, and has no visibility into the backend his technical cofounder owns. That suggests **the map as
  a shared language between a non-technical founder (who views and asks) and a technical cofounder (who acts).**
  Promise "you'll see where V2 will hurt", not "you'll know it scales".
- **The integration interviewee is the clearest signal.** He had to change a client's data integration, asked GPT how
  the workflow worked, and got a wall of text instead of a diagram. *Consultants working in client codebases* may be a
  sharp segment: they hit this on every new client.
- **The third person** plans heavily and says AI implements well "but…". The note cut off. **Follow up**: this is either
  the toughest customer or evidence that the pain is smaller for disciplined planners.
- **The bar to clear is "ask Claude for a Mermaid diagram".** That's free and solves maybe 60% of "wall of text". Codemap
  has to win on things people notice: claims checked against the code, click-through to the code, the same drawing every
  time, and **showing what's missing**.

## 4. What the user wants from the interface (direct feedback)

- **Point at anything and ask.** Select a box, an arrow or a region; answers appear next to what was selected.
- **Plain English first.** Translating code into concepts *is* the value. Three depths: Concept, How it works, Code.
  Define jargon. Use a small concrete example from their own code.
- **A real graph:** areas as containers, steps inside, labeled arrows between them. An early design with lane rows of
  blocks was rejected as "unintuitive, not an actual graph".
- **A walkthrough written with each map,** because a graph alone is hard to start reading. Stops go in the order that
  makes sense to a newcomer, and you can ask at every stop.
- **No "guess what happens next" prompts.** That idea was rejected.
- **The agent can fix things from the map**, not just explain them (see decision 5).
- **Model-agnostic is wanted.** The simplest version: codemap runs its own Claude explainer, and any coding agent
  launches it.
- **Learning from walkthroughs:** a diagram of the user's own vibecoded architecture lost them. Every diagram needs its
  question and a line of context on top, 5 to 7 boxes at first with details on click, and plain labels.

## 5. Design decisions and why

1. **v1: Claude explores, a plain program checks.** No deterministic graph engine yet, because it isn't needed for
   "ask, get a map". Claude explores with Read/Grep/Glob and returns the map in a fixed format. `check()` re-reads every
   cited line and verifies calls, requests and imports against code facts. Later, the engine can replace the explorer
   behind the same format.
2. **The map format (`packages/core/src/format.ts`) is the one-way door.** Everything else is replaceable. Statuses are
   never stored; they're computed on every check.
3. **"Nothing does X" is a claim with proof.** Absences carry the search that proves them, and the checker reruns it.
   The missing connection is the bug people care about, and only a graph that can show absences can show it.
4. **Codemap runs its own Claude explainer,** separate from the user's coding chat. It works with any agent and keeps
   explanation quality consistent. It can read the whole repo: the map is a starting point, not a fence. Anything it
   adds is drawn only if the checker confirms it.
5. **Fixes:** Claude proposes. The fix is drawn as a green dashed arrow next to the exact diff. Nothing changes until
   approval. Then codemap writes exactly that diff, refusing if the files changed since the proposal, re-checks the map,
   and offers Undo. Only one agent edits at a time. If codemap is ever connected to the user's coding chat, that agent
   makes the edit instead.
6. **Delivery:** the basic version works everywhere through a skill, the `codemap` CLI and a browser tab. Optional
   upgrades (not built):
   - **Channels:** Claude Code only, research preview. An MCP server pushes the user's question into the running chat.
   - **MCP Apps:** Cursor, VS Code Copilot, ChatGPT, Claude Desktop. The viewer embeds in the chat, and `ui/message` sends
     questions.
   - **Codex:** no documented way to push into a running session. Its desktop app has a Browser with an Annotate picker
     and WebMCP, which might allow something similar; untested.
7. **Local only:** binds to 127.0.0.1, a token is required, Host and Origin are checked, and secrets are never read.

## 6. Graphify, for comparison (github.com/Graphify-Labs/graphify, read at v0.9.97)

- **Agent-facing.** Code goes to a graph through tree-sitter (no LLM). Query is keyword match, then BFS spreading in every
  direction. Clusters (Leiden) are named after their busiest node. Updates happen after commits, asynchronously, in
  seconds. There are no ordered flows, no fetch → route links, and no events or queues for JS. Its "benchmark" measures
  tokens, not task success. Graphify Cloud (YC S26) adds architecture rules.
- **Ideas worth borrowing:**
  - An edge counts as EXTRACTED only with import evidence; ambiguous matches are dropped rather than guessed.
  - Edges belong to the file they come from, so a change evicts only that file's edges.
  - Keep cluster IDs stable between rebuilds.
  - Stamp the graph with `built_at_commit`.
  - Hook messages phrased as facts, not commands. They found imperative wording gets ignored as prompt injection.
- **Don't build on it.** Codemap's edge is everything it lacks.

## 7. What's built (verified)

- **Tests:** four packages, 102 tests, no model calls.
- **Viewer:** tested in Chrome with scripted Claude (`npm run preview`): making a map, the walkthrough, select and ask,
  a follow-up that adds checked steps, a fix (approve, reload, undo).
- **Real Claude, on the care-app fixture:**
  - The map came back 20 of 20 confirmed on the first pass, for about $0.21.
  - It also found a bug nobody planted: nothing ever starts the nightly job.
  - A real question cost about $0.14 and added two confirmed gaps.
  - A real fix cost about $0.24, was approved and applied, and re-checked 22 of 22.
- **Demo frontend:** `examples/care-app-ui/index.html`, the patient app as staff see it. Convert a patient and no welcome
  email arrives, even though the automation is active.

## 8. Not built yet, and next steps

- **Questions, answers and fix proposals live in server memory** and are lost on restart; maps are saved to disk.
- **Hand-off to the user's coding agent** (channels / MCP Apps) and an MCP `publish_map` tool for agents that explore on
  their own.
- **Big repos are untested.** The head-start scan reads the whole repo.
- **Next, in order:**
  1. **Run Phase 0 with the integration interviewee:** his real question, codemap vs "Claude + Mermaid" side by side.
  2. Try codemap on a real repo, or a fresh Scout copy (`../scout-run`; never `../scout-agent`).
  3. Persist sessions.
  4. Channels hand-off in Claude Code.
  5. MCP Apps.
- **Later (Phase 3 of the plan):**
  - A fast graph engine with updates on every edit (incremental, LSP-style).
  - Live agent activity on the map.
  - "Working somewhere you haven't explored" and a per-user explored-regions map.
  - "This step was patched 5 times this week" counters. That's the *band-aid detector*, and it needs a time dimension.

## 9. Gotchas that cost time

- **Agent SDK (`@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk` 0.3.296), verified from its types:**
  - The call is `query({ prompt, options: { cwd, model, tools, allowedTools, permissionMode: 'dontAsk', settingSources: [], strictMcpConfig, outputFormat: { type: 'json_schema', schema }, resume, hooks } })`.
  - The answer arrives as `structured_output` on the `result` message.
  - PreToolUse hooks can return `permissionDecision` and `updatedInput`.
  - Auth is an API key or the Claude Code login.
- **React Flow 12:**
  - With controlled nodes, measurements live on `getInternalNode(id).measured`, not on your node objects.
  - Nodes that aren't selectable or draggable get `pointer-events: none` unless `onNodeClick` is set. Steps carry
    `nopan` so a pan doesn't swallow clicks.
- **ELK:** spacing options apply per container, so each area repeats them.
- **Chrome automation:**
  - A hidden tab renders no React Flow edges and drops input; check `document.visibilityState` and drive the page with
    in-page events.
  - The first click after a navigation is often dropped.
- **zsh `echo` mangles backslashes in JSON.** Write curl output to a file instead.
- **Channels with a custom server:**
  - Launch with `claude --dangerously-load-development-channels server:<name>`.
  - Claude Code won't register a channel server on MCP protocol 2026-07-28; `MCP_SDK_GENERATION=v1` works around it.
  - The page needs its own sender check (a token): an ungated channel is a prompt-injection risk.

## 10. Links

- Design spec, current: [Codemap v1 Design](https://claude.ai/artifact/55L8tokprGe61qtfpDXJ5h)
- Longer-term plan with the engine: [Point-and-Ask Architecture](https://claude.ai/artifact/7hWiwFyugpB6hT6x3DKoJs)
- Graphify vs. ours: [Two Code Graphs Compared](https://claude.ai/artifact/8u9v9BAXW4pTLkz72exhv5)
- Early concept frames (Figma): https://www.figma.com/design/i8aTiDS47Eb68QeoKvQopW
- Hackathon origin, reference only: `../Speedhacks-project` (the Interpretability harness)
- Claude Code channels: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/channels · MCP Apps client matrix:
  https://modelcontextprotocol.io/extensions/client-matrix
````

```text
/** A fake agent that replies from a script, in order, and records every request. */
export function scriptedAgent(replies: ((req: AgentRequest) => unknown)[]): Agent & { calls: AgentRequest[] } {
  const calls: AgentRequest[] = [];
  const agent = (async (req: AgentRequest): Promise<AgentResponse> => {
    calls.push(req);
    const reply = replies[calls.length - 1];
    if (!reply) throw new Error(`no scripted reply for call ${calls.length}`);
    req.onProgress?.({ kind: 'read', text: 'Reading src/patients/service.ts' });
    return { output: reply(req), sessionId: `session-${calls.length}`, cost: 0.01 };
  }) as Agent & { calls: AgentRequest[] };
  agent.calls = calls;
  return agent;
}
```

```text
const withQuestion = (output: unknown, question: string) =>
  output && typeof output === 'object' ? { ...(output as Record<string, unknown>), version: 1, question } : output;

export async function makeMap(o: MakeOptions): Promise<MakeResult> {
  const status = (text: string) => o.onProgress?.({ kind: 'status', text });
  status('Scanning the code for ways in, routes and tables');
  const hints = await headStart(o.root);
  status('Claude is exploring the code');
  const run = (prompt: string, resume: string | null) =>
    o.agent({ prompt, schema: MAP_SCHEMA, cwd: o.root, resume, model: o.model, onProgress: o.onProgress, signal: o.signal });

  let res = await run(makerPrompt(o.question, hints.text), null);
  let cost = res.cost ?? 0;
  let rounds = 1;
  let best: { map: CodeMap; report: CheckReport } | null = null;
  let lastProblems: string[] = [];

  for (let attempt = 0; ; attempt++) {
    const parsed = parseMap(withQuestion(res.output, o.question));
    let repair: string | null = null;
    if (!parsed.ok) {
      lastProblems = parsed.problems;
      repair = shapeRepairPrompt(parsed.problems);
    } else {
      status('Checking every claim against the code');
      const report = check(parsed.map, o.root);
      if (!best || report.summary.unconfirmed < best.report.summary.unconfirmed) best = { map: parsed.map, report };
      status(`${report.summary.confirmed} of ${report.summary.claims} claims confirmed`);
      if (report.summary.unconfirmed > 0) repair = evidenceRepairPrompt(report);
    }
    if (!repair || attempt >= (o.repairs ?? 2)) break;
    status(parsed.ok ? 'Asking Claude to fix the claims that didn\'t check out' : 'Asking Claude to fix the map\'s structure');
    res = await run(repair, res.sessionId);
    cost += res.cost ?? 0;
    rounds++;
  }
  if (!best) throw new Error(`Claude's map couldn't be read: ${lastProblems.slice(0, 5).join('; ')}`);
  return { ...best, sessionId: res.sessionId, cost, rounds };
}
```

````bash
## How the pieces fit

- **Make** (`server/src/maker.ts`): `headStart` (a `@codemap/facts` scan, `hints.ts`) seeds the prompt → `Agent` returns
  JSON against `MAP_SCHEMA` → `parseMap` → `check`. Shape errors or unconfirmed claims get up to two repair rounds on
  the same session; the best-checked map wins. Prompts live in `prompts.ts`, output schemas in `schemas.ts`.
- **Ask** (`explainer.ts`): answers may carry additions (merged with `addToMap` in `core/src/edit.ts`) and a fix.
  Additions that don't pass `check` are dropped before the map is returned, not shown as unconfirmed.
- **Fix** (`fixes.ts`): `proposeFix` records file hashes → `applyFix` writes only if they still match →
  `connectAfterFix` draws the new edge and closes the gaps it fills → `undoFix`.
- **Serve** (`server.ts`, `store.ts`): maps persist as `<repo>/.codemap/maps/<id>.json`; jobs, answers and fix
  proposals are in memory only. Binds 127.0.0.1, requires a token, checks Host and Origin; the viewer gets job
  progress over the WebSocket.
- Server tests use `scriptedAgent` and `copyCareApp` from `packages/server/test/helpers.ts`; follow that pattern
````

```text
# CLAUDE.md

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

## codemap

A map you can point at and ask about, for code you didn't write yourself. Read `README.md`, then `HANDOFF.md` (who it's
for, what users asked for, the decisions and why, what's next, gotchas). The design lives in the "Codemap v1 Design"
artifact (link in both).

## Rules

- **The model writes, the code decides.** Nothing reaches the screen without passing `check()` in `@codemap/core`. A
  model never sets a claim's status; the checker computes it from the repo every time.
- **One checker, every call site.** Publishing a map, every answer, reopening a saved map, and after a fix all call the
  same `check()`. Don't fork its logic.
- **"Nothing does X" is a claim too.** Absences carry the search that proves them, and the checker reruns it.
- **The map format is the one-way door.** Change `packages/core/src/format.ts` deliberately, with tests. Everything
  else (generator, viewer, explainer) is replaceable behind it.
- **Read-only unless approved.** Codemap writes to a target repo only under `.codemap/`, and edits product code only
```

- **Two easy-to-miss facts:**
  - Only the viewer gets built. The other packages run straight from their TypeScript source, so after changing the viewer you need `npm run build` before `npm run codemap`. `preview` rebuilds for you.
  - Vitest only finds tests named `test/*.test.ts` directly in each package's `test/` folder, not in subfolders.
- **A new "How the pieces fit" section:**
  - **Make:** the code scan's head start, then Claude, then the format check and `check()`, with up to two repair rounds; the map with the most confirmed claims wins.
  - **Ask:** anything Claude adds to the map that fails `check()` is dropped, not shown with a "?".
  - **Fix:** propose → apply (only if the files haven't changed) → draw the new connection → undo.
  - **Serve:** maps are saved to disk, while jobs, answers and fix proposals live only in server memory.
  - **Tests:** server tests use the scripted Claude helpers in `packages/server/test/helpers.ts`.

I left out what `HANDOFF.md` already covers (the Agent SDK, React Flow and ELK gotchas), since `CLAUDE.md` already points to it.

There are no Cursor, Copilot, Codex or Gemini config files in the repo, so there was nothing to import.
